practical.title: Analyze and Implement Linear Search for Strings
practical.sourceActivity: Analyze and Implement Linear Search for Strings

files.description: Runnable C starter file for the practical.

tasks.title: Scene 1 — Observe & Understand: Run the baseline program
tasks.instruction: Compile and run the provided main.c. Read the output and observe the two results: one target that exists and one that does not. Notice the exact messages printed and which indices are returned.
tasks.narratorGuide: Hello — run this working program first so you get a concrete sense of what 'linear search for strings' prints and returns. Watching the program output maps the abstract idea (compare each element to the target) to real, observable behavior: you’ll see a found index for "Charlie" and a not-found message for "Frank". Next we'll make a tiny source edit so you can feel how a small change affects output.

tasks.title: Scene 2 — Modify & Experiment: Change a target (1-2 line edit)
tasks.instruction: Edit main.c: change the line assigning target2 to search for an existing name (one-line change). Recompile and run. Observe the new output and confirm the index printed matches the element's position.
tasks.narratorGuide: Now you'll make a tiny source edit — just change the target string for the second search. This shows that the algorithm's control flow is driven directly by input: if the target exists, the function returns its index; otherwise it returns -1. After you change the target and recompile, compare the printed index with the element's position in the array to validate your understanding.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — Build & Integrate: Case-insensitive search (add/verify)
tasks.instruction: We included a working case-insensitive search implementation (linear_search_strings_ci and ci_compare). Run the program with the 'ci' argument to exercise it. Confirm the program prints a found message for a lower-case target.
tasks.narratorGuide: Case sensitivity matters: user input may not match the exact letter case stored in data. The ci_compare helper demonstrates a common solution: normalize characters before comparing. Run the program in 'ci' mode to confirm that 'charlie' (lowercase) resolves to the same index as 'Charlie'. This scene teaches you how small modular functions let you adapt an algorithm's behavior without rewriting core logic.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — Verify & Extend: Instrument comparisons and explore string-length impact
tasks.instruction: Run the compiled program with the 'verbose' argument: ./main verbose. Read the three lines printed; they show index, element_comparisons, and char_comparisons for 'Alice', 'Charlie', and 'Frank'. Use these concrete counts to answer the Big O analysis questions.
tasks.narratorGuide: Instrumenting the algorithm bridges theory and practice. The verbose mode prints counts you can map to Big O ideas: the element comparisons correspond to n in the worst case, while char comparisons reveal how string length influences total work. For example, comparing equal strings requires examining each character; this multiplies the cost. After observing the numbers, answer the two analysis questions: best-case and worst-case complexities, and explain how string length factors in via strcmp.

safety.learnerWarning: This practical runs in an isolated workspace. Do not use real credentials or production resources.

cleanup.instructions: Discard the isolated workspace after completion.
